alignment.note: All three traditions mark the adversative transition: Greek postpositive δέ and Syriac ܕܝܢ both follow the subject pronoun, whereas the Latin At illi fronts the conjunction in classical fashion — a stylistic word-order difference without semantic weight.

The Greek high point (·) and the Latin colon (:) both introduce direct speech; the Syriac transmits the same clause boundary without an orthographic mark, so the punctuation must be inferred. The Greek index is shared with its verb-token since the raised point is affixed to ἔκραξαν·.

Greek and Syriac express the command with a single imperative verb bearing a pronominal object (σταύρωσον αὐτόν conflated into ܙܩܘܦܝܗܝ, 'crucify-him'); the Latin separates the imperative Crucifige from the explicit accusative pronoun eum, a typical analytic rendering of the Semitic/Greek synthetic form.
